geo:GSE326654.title: in vivo human embryonic spinal cord atlas validates stem cell-derived human dorsal interneurons and reveals ASD spinal signatures [day27NMP_scRNAseq]
geo:GSE326654.study_title: in vivo human embryonic spinal cord atlas validates stem cell-derived human dorsal interneurons and reveals ASD spinal signatures [day27NMP_scRNAseq]
geo:GSE326654.notes: resp_score=0; gdstype=Expression profiling by high throughput sequencing
geo:GSE326654.description: Spinal cord injuries (SCI) result in the loss of motor and sensory function. We are working towards restoring sensation by developing directed differentiation protocols to generate dorsal spinal interneurons (dIs; dI1-dI6) from human embryonic stem cells (hESCs). Here, we present an improved method that produces human dIs via a neuromesodermal progenitor state, the physiological intermediate for spinal cord development. We show that retinoic acid (RA), bone morphogenetic protein 4 (BMP4) and growth differentiation factor (GDF) 11 direct dI identity, while GDF11 and extended time in culture promotes posterior spinal identities. Together, these protocols generate the full complement of dorsal subtypes along the entire anterior-posterior axis of the spinal cord. To benchmark in vitro-derived dIs, we constructed a single-cell RNA-Seq atlas of the human embryonic spinal cord and used it to show that hESC-derived dIs closely match their endogenous counterparts. The atlas also reveals that the dI4/dI5 populations dramatically expand in comparison with the other spinal lineages. Moreover, they have mechanosensory circuit signatures linked to autism spectrum disorder, implicating spinal circuits in autistic phenotypes.

geo:GSE336853.title: New taxonomy based on individual patient-reported response trajectories defines ulcerative colitis endotypes and reveals vascular inflammation as a mechanism for vedolizumab nonresponse.
geo:GSE336853.study_title: New taxonomy based on individual patient-reported response trajectories defines ulcerative colitis endotypes and reveals vascular inflammation as a mechanism for vedolizumab nonresponse.
geo:GSE336853.description: A major barrier to precision medicine for ulcerative colitis (UC) is the inability to predict and mechanistically explain treatment responses. Using daily patient-reported outcomes from a phase 3b comparative trial of 768 participants, we identified four distinct patient response trajectory groups for vedolizumab (anti-integrin) and adalimumab (antitumor necrosis factor) in UC. Validation in a second phase 3 trial of 591 participants linked vedolizumab trajectories to long-term disease complications. Bulk, single-cell, and spatial, transcriptomics and proteomics, identified vascular inflammation to be associated with vedolizumab nonresponse via SPP1+ monocytes and the angiopoetin-2 pathway. In a real-world cohort of 3,187 patients with UC, concomitant use of renin-angiotensin system inhibitors (modulators of vascular inflammation and angiopoietin-2 signaling) was associated with reduced long-term complications for vedolizumab but not anti-cytokine therapies. These findings define a response trajectory-based taxonomy, and endotype-specific outcome prediction, implicating vascular inflammation as a drug-specific and targetable resistance pathway for vedolizumab in UC.

geo:GSE343941.title: Cuproptosis eliminates cancer persister cells that survive ferroptosis
geo:GSE343941.study_title: Cuproptosis eliminates cancer persister cells that survive ferroptosis
geo:GSE343941.notes: resp_score=0; gdstype=Expression profiling by high throughput sequencing
geo:GSE343941.description: Cancer persister cells survive drug treatment, adapt, and seed relapse. Targeting persister cells may therefore prevent resistance. Though persister cells survive drug-induced apoptosis, they are sensitized to ferroptosis which can be induced by GPX4 inhibitors. However, GPX4 inhibition does not kill every persister cell. Therefore, there is a need to identify other ways to eliminate persister cells. Here, by exploring the mechanism by which the alcohol use disorder drug disulfiram kills persister cells, we discovered that persister cells are generally sensitized to cuproptosis induced by copper ionophores. We compared persister cell cuproptosis to ferroptosis and found they have fundamentally distinct requirements for reactive oxygen species, copper or iron usage, and opposing roles for oxidative phosphorylation. Consequently, persister cells that survive ferroptosis are sensitized to cuproptosis. Therefore, persister cells can be efficiently eliminated by sequentially treating with ferroptosis and cuproptosis inducers.
